"Wooly Bully" is a song originally recorded by rock and roll band Sam the Sham and the Pharaohs in 1964. Based on a standard 12-bar blues progression, it was written by the band's frontman, Domingo "Sam" Samudio. It was released as a single on the small Memphis-based XL label (#906) in 1964 and was picked up in 1965 by MGM. The song was recorded at Sam C. Phillips Recording Studio at 639 Madison Avenue in Memphis, the successor to Phillips' original Sun Studio.

sections.heading: Chart history
sections.wikitext:
"Wooly Bully" was the band's first and biggest hit song. It became a worldwide success, selling three million copies and reaching No. 2 on the American [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]] chart on June 5–12, 1965. They were kept from reaching the top spot by [[The Beach Boys]]' "[[Help Me, Rhonda]]"<ref name=":2">{{cite web| url= http://www.billboard.com/charts/1965-06-05/hot-100 |title= The Hot 100: Week of June 5, 1965 |website =Billboard.com |access-date=January 8, 2012}}</ref> and [[The Supremes]]' "[[Back in My Arms Again]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.billboard.com/charts/1965-06-12/hot-100 |title= The Hot 100: Week of June 12, 1965 |website =Billboard.com|access-date=February 6, 2012}}</ref> "Wooly Bully" went to No. 31 on the [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|Hot Rhythm & Blues Singles]] chart.<ref name=":3">{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942-2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=510}}</ref> The song also reached No. 2 on the Canadian [[CHUM Chart]]s.<ref name=":13" />

The song was the first American record to sell a million copies during the [[British Invasion]] and was influenced by the British rock sound which was mixed with traditional Mexican-American [[conjunto]] rhythms.<ref>{{citation |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d3vlqWvTDfgC&pg=PA207 |title=The history of Texas music |first=Gary|last=Hartman| publisher= Texas A&M University Press| year= 2008| isbn= 9781603440028}}</ref><ref>{{citation |magazine=Billboard |page=10 |date= September 25, 1965 |volume=77 |number=39 |title=MGM has boom months}}</ref> It stayed in the Hot 100 for 18 weeks, the longest time for any song in 1965, and was nominated for a [[Grammy Award]]. It was named ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'s'' [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1965|number-one song of the year]] despite never reaching No. 1 on a weekly Hot 100, making this the first occurrence of such an event on the Hot 100.<ref name=":5">{{Cite magazine|date=2021-12-02|title=Year-End Charts, Billboard Hot 100 Songs|url=https://www.billboard.com/charts/year-end/2021/hot-100-songs/|access-date=2021-12-02|magazine=Billboard|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|last1=Trust|first1=Gary|last2=Caulfield|first2=Keith|date=2021-12-02|title=The Year In Charts 2021: Dua Lipa's 'Levitating' Is the No. 1 Billboard Hot 100 Song of the Year|url=https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/dua-lipa-levitating-2021-hot-100-top-song-year-in-charts-1235004941/|access-date=2021-12-02|magazine=Billboard|language=en-US}}</ref> On August 5, 1965, the single was certified as gold by the RIAA.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.riaa.com/goldandplatinumdata.php?artist=%22Wooly+Bully%22|title= RIAA Gold & Platinum Searchable Database – Wooly Bully |publisher= [[Recording Industry Association of America]]|access-date= 16 October 2015}}</ref> It was later included on the band's 1965 album ''[[Wooly Bully (Album)|Wooly Bully]]''.
sections.text:
"Wooly Bully" was the band's first and biggest hit song. It became a worldwide success, selling three million copies and reaching No. 2 on the American Hot 100 chart on June 5–12, 1965. They were kept from reaching the top spot by The Beach Boys' "Help Me, Rhonda" and The Supremes' "Back in My Arms Again". "Wooly Bully" went to No. 31 on the Hot Rhythm & Blues Singles chart. The song also reached No. 2 on the Canadian CHUM Charts.

The song was the first American record to sell a million copies during the British Invasion and was influenced by the British rock sound which was mixed with traditional Mexican-American conjunto rhythms. It stayed in the Hot 100 for 18 weeks, the longest time for any song in 1965, and was nominated for a Grammy Award. It was named Billboard's number-one song of the year despite never reaching No. 1 on a weekly Hot 100, making this the first occurrence of such an event on the Hot 100. On August 5, 1965, the single was certified as gold by the RIAA. It was later included on the band's 1965 album Wooly Bully.

sections.heading: Title and lyrics
sections.wikitext:
"Wooly Bully" is a reworking of the 1962 tune "Hully Gully Now" on the Dallas-based Gay Shel label by Big Bo & The Arrows (vocal by Little Smitty), which was based on [[Junior Parker]]'s "Feelin' Good". The song was given the green light after Samudio rewrote the lyrics to replace "Hully Gully" with "Wooly Bully" and a few additional lyrical changes. Samudio retained the "watch it, watch it now" refrain from the original version.<ref name="TheBillboardbookof#2singles">{{cite book | first= Christopher G.|last= Feldman|title= The Billboard Book of #2 Singles|page=[https://archive.org/details/billboardbookofn00chri/page/79 79]|publisher=Watson-Guptill|year=2000|isbn= 0-8230-7695-4|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/billboardbookofn00chri/page/79}}</ref>

The lyrics of "Wooly Bully" were hard to understand; in consequence, some radio stations banned the song.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://americansongwriter.com/behind-the-song-wooly-bully-by-sam-the-sham-the-pharoahs/ |title=Behind the Song: "Wooly Bully" by Sam The Sham & The Pharoahs |last=Zollo |first=Paul |date=15 October 2021 |website=American Songwriter}}</ref> The lyrics describe a conversation between "Mattie" and "Hattie" concerning the "Wooly Bully" (a creature which Mattie describes as "a thing she saw [that] had two big horns and a wooly jaw" – that is, an [[American bison]]) and the desirability of developing dancing skills, although no attempt is made to [[:wikt:synthesize|synthesize]] these divergent topics. The warning "Let's not be L-7" means "Let's not be [[square (slang)|square]]", from the shape formed by the fingers making an ''L'' on one hand and a ''7'' on the other.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://greensdictofslang.com/entry/bplu7ri|title=L-7|website=Green’s Dictionary of Slang|access-date=October 23, 2021}}</ref> Sam the Sham underscores the [[Tejano music|Tex-Mex]] nature of the song by counting out the rhythm in [[Spanish language|Spanish]] and English ("Uno! Dos! One, two, tres, cuatro!"), and the characteristic simple organ [[riff]]ing, with a [[tenor saxophone]] solo in the middle. According to Samudio, "The count down part of the song was also not planned. I was just goofing around and counted off in Tex-Mex. It just blew everybody away, and actually, I wanted it taken off the record. We did three takes, all of them different, and they took the first take and released it."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.classicbands.com/samsham.html|title=Sam The Sham|website=ClassicBands.com|access-date=January 8, 2012}}</ref>

The warning "Let's not be L-7" means "Let's not be square", from the shape formed by the fingers making an L on one hand and a 7 on the other. Sam the Sham underscores the Tex-Mex nature of the song by counting out the rhythm in Spanish and English ("Uno! Dos! One, two, tres, cuatro!"), and the characteristic simple organ riffing, with a tenor saxophone solo in the middle. According to Samudio, "The count down part of the song was also not planned. Awards
sections.wikitext: In 2009, the original 1965 release of the song on the MGM label by [[Sam the Sham and the Pharaohs]] was inducted into the [[Grammy Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.grammy.com/awards/hall-of-fame-award#w|title=GRAMMY Hall Of Fame | Hall of Fame Artists | GRAMMY.com|website=grammy.com}}</ref>
sections.text: In 2009, the original 1965 release of the song on the MGM label by Sam the Sham and the Pharaohs was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

sections.heading: Commercial usage
sections.wikitext: Starting in the [[2025–26 Utah Mammoth season|2025–26 season]], the [[Utah Mammoth]] of the [[National Hockey League]], began using Wooly Bully as their win song. Wooly Bully is played at the conclusion of every home game where Utah wins, in regulation or overtime.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Instagram |url=https://www.instagram.com/p/DLqWttwB0at/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link |access-date=2026-04-08 |website=www.instagram.com}}</ref>
sections.text: Starting in the 2025–26 season, the Utah Mammoth of the National Hockey League, began using Wooly Bully as their win song. Wooly Bully is played at the conclusion of every home game where Utah wins, in regulation or overtime.
